name: Mumbai
_comment: Every number below carries a source id (see 'sources') and a kind: measured = published figure; derived = arithmetic on published figures (formula shown in the dashboard); assumption = our modelling choice, stated openly and editable here. Nothing in this file is tuned to make any policy win.

zones._note: Distribution licensee areas. BEST serves the island city; the suburbs were Reliance Energy's area in 2005 and are Adani Electricity's today (Tata Power overlaps citywide). Census groups wards the same way.

supply_margin.note: Before a disaster strikes, available supply is taken as 3% above demand (no load shedding on a normal day).

noise_frac.note: ±2% random variation in available supply per 15-minute step (seeded, reproducible).

shape.note: Daily demand as a fraction of the day's peak. The 05:00 trough (2,140 ÷ 3,944 = 0.543) and the afternoon peak are from the Maharashtra SLDC October 2024 report; the in-between points are a smooth interpolation we chose (assumption).

disasters.name: Grid islanding failure
disasters.summary: Two 400 kV lines feeding Mumbai tripped within seven minutes. The city's islanding scheme could not hold a 1,000 MW drop, Trombay and Uran units tripped, and 2,600 MW of load was lost, 2,200 MW of it in Mumbai. Only Adani's Dahanu-fed island (about 400 MW) stayed up.

demand.note: Demand at the moment of islanding was over 2,800 MW.

loss.note: Loss and onset are measured. Restoration began at noon and most areas were back after about two hours, the last after up to 15 hours; the 85%-by-14:00 shape is our reading of those reports.

timeline.text: 400 kV Kalwa–Padghe line 2 trips on an R-phase fault
400 kV Kalwa–Kharghar line (carrying 900 MW) trips: conductor snap
Kharghar transformers trip; islanding fails; 2,600 MW of load lost
Central main line rail power restored

record.value: COVID hospitals kept running on backup

disasters.name: Monsoon deluge
disasters.date: Tuesday 26 July 2005, replayed on today's grid
disasters.summary: 944 mm of rain fell on Santacruz in 24 hours, the wettest day on record. Local trains stopped by 14:30. Reliance Energy, then the suburban licensee, shut feeders on a state safety directive, switching off over 150 substations, and the suburbs stayed dark until the water receded. We apply that pattern to today's demand: the suburban licensee's share (Adani, 2,070 of 4,041 MW) is switched off from the evening.

demand.note: No published July demand curve: we use the October 2024 peak day as a typical non-summer day.

loss.note: Share = 2,070 ÷ 4,041 MW (Adani's part of city demand). The shutdown came 'from the evening'; 19:00 is our reading.

timeline.text: Severe storm and deluge hit the city
Local trains stop on waterlogged tracks
Suburban feeders shut down for public safety

record.label: Phone users cut off
record.value: 5 million mobile and 2.3 million landline users, over 4 hours

disasters.name: Cyclone Tauktae
disasters.summary: An extremely severe cyclone passed offshore. Colaba recorded 102 km/h winds by 11:00 and Mumbai's highest gust on record, 114 km/h, around 14:00. Falling trees tripped Adani feeders, 2,426 streetlights failed and waterlogged areas were switched off as a precaution. We found no published figure for megawatts lost, so the size of the loss here is our assumption: use the intensity slider to explore it.

loss.note: ASSUMPTION: 12% of demand lost at the peak of the storm (14:00–17:00), ramping in from 11:00 and mostly restored by 21:00.

timeline.text: 114 km/h gust: highest ever recorded in Mumbai
Trees fall on cables; Adani feeders trip; waterlogged areas switched off

disasters.name: Forecast: 2020 failure at the record peak
disasters.date: What if 12 October 2020 had happened at 15:30 on 9 June 2023?
disasters.summary: A forward-looking stress test built only from recorded numbers: the same 2,200 MW loss and the same restoration pace as 2020, but striking at the city's record 4,129 MW peak in the afternoon heat. Nothing like it has happened yet; this is the scenario planners should prepare for.

loss.note: 2020's measured loss and restoration timing, shifted to start at the 2023 peak.

timeline.text: Assumed: the 2020 trip sequence repeats; 2,200 MW lost

forecast.note: Each forecast runs 24 versions of the day. Each version draws the loss size within ±15% and the restoration time within ±30% of the recorded values, plus its own supply noise. We report the middle (median) outcome and the 10th–90th percentile range.
